name: Pantocrin

card.summary: A Russian alcohol extract of deer antler velvet, taken as a tonic for stamina and recovery that people link to training and a fitter look.
card.note: Antler products are discussed in sport for possible IGF-1 and contamination concerns; anaphylaxis after injection reported in a 1975 case.

quick.overview:
Pantocrin is an extract of the soft, velvet-covered antlers of deer, produced in Russia from the 1930s to the 1980s and still sold there. It is regarded in the adaptogen tradition as a tonic for stamina, recovery and vitality, which proponents connect to training capacity and a healthier physique.

Animal studies report effects on reproductive hormones and growth, and a 1990 paper reported radioprotective effects in mice. A 2012 review found that claims of benefits for human conditions lack solid support from human trials.
quick.how: Pantocrin is sold as liquid extract, tablets or ampules. Antler velvet more broadly is used as a supplement or spray by athletes and lifters; general practice is courses taken over weeks.
quick.risks: A 1975 case report describes anaphylactic shock after subcutaneous administration. The US FDA has sent warning letters over disease claims for velvet antler, and sports bodies have flagged deer antler products over possible IGF-1 and contamination, with MLB banning the spray in 2011.

lead: Pantocrin (also pantocrine) is a Russian alcohol extract of deer antler velvet, produced from the 1930s to the 1980s and sold under that name.[1] It is used as a general tonic, and in lifting and wellness circles as a recovery and vitality aid, aiming at more training capacity and a fitter physique.

Velvet antler is the cartilage-like early-growth antler of deer, elk, moose and caribou; in traditional Chinese medicine it is dried, sliced or powdered, and New Zealand is the largest producer.[1] A 2012 review found that claims of benefit for any human condition lack solid support from human trials.[1]
Research on pantocrin itself is mostly Russian and Japanese experimental work in animals and cells.

chain: Antler extract taken as an adaptogen tonic
Claimed support for stamina, recovery and hormones
angle.text: Users take it as a general tonic, expecting better recovery and vigor. The link to appearance runs through training and wellbeing and rests on proponents' claims.

paras: Russia produced the alcohol extract of velvet antler from the 1930s through the 1980s under the name Pantocrin.[1] The Russian drug registry lists a red deer antler extract product.[2]

The FDA sent warning letters over disease-treatment claims; supplements may be sold without disease claims. Deer antler spray caused controversy in professional sport: MLB banned it in 2011 over possible contamination, and WADA lifted a ban in 2013 while warning it may contain IGF-1.[1]

No controlled human trials of pantocrin for appearance or training were identified. Animal and lab work includes a study in which pantocrin stimulated sexual behavior in winter in rodents, attributed to weak gonadotropic activity;[3] reports on reproductive hormones in male rats;[4] radioprotection in irradiated cells and mice;[5] and a cattle study using pantocrine among adaptogens for live weight gain.[6] A 1975 case report described anaphylactic shock after subcutaneous administration.[7]

timeline.event: Soviet production of the antler extract begins.[1]
WADA lifts ban but warns of IGF-1.[1]
